bibliographic.title: Observability for LLM apps: what to log, privacy-safe telemetry, KPIs
bibliographic.venue: Frontiers in Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence
bibliographic.citation_apa: Maderamitla, P., & Katragadda, S. R. (2026). Observability for LLM apps: what to log, privacy-safe telemetry, KPIs. Frontiers in Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.32996/fcsai

methodology.method_family: conceptual framework development drawing on software observability and MLOps best practices
methodology.technology_context: LLM applications with conversational interfaces, intelligent assistants, decision-support systems, tool invocation, retrieval systems, and orchestration pipelines; observability via logs, metrics, traces, and privacy-safe telemetry

eligibility.decision_rationale: The article directly addresses observability, auditable logging, privacy-preserving telemetry, and operational KPIs for LLM applications, explicitly linking these practices to governance risks, safety compliance, and enterprise deployment. It proposes a model-agnostic observability framework with interaction, execution, performance, and safety layers, which aligns closely with the review focus on operational/technical governance, monitoring, auditability, privacy, and compliance in LLM-based systems.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only front matter/page 1 text was provided; full methods, KPI definitions, framework validation, limitations, and regulated-domain treatment require manual verification. Metadata also shows inconsistent DOI values (10.32996/fcsai vs 10.32996/jcsts.2026.5.4.2).

appraisal.notes: Based on available text, the study is a conceptual framework paper rather than an empirical evaluation. Objectives are clearly stated, and privacy-by-design considerations are articulated, but no empirical sample, data collection protocol, analytical procedure, or limitations section is visible in the excerpt provided.

cerqual.explanation: The abstract and introduction present a coherent governance-relevant observability framework for LLM apps, but confidence is limited because only page 1 was supplied, no empirical validation is described, and adequacy of the proposed KPI set and privacy controls cannot be fully assessed from the excerpt.

coding.theme: Model-agnostic observability and governance-oriented telemetry for LLM applications
coding.subtheme: Privacy-preserving logging and operational KPI design for enterprise LLM systems

synthesis.main_claim: Traditional software observability is inadequate for LLM applications because probabilistic behavior, prompt dependency, and complex orchestration make semantic correctness, behavioral consistency, and governance risks hard to monitor; the authors propose a conceptual, model-agnostic observability framework covering auditable data selection, privacy-preserving telemetry, and LLM-specific operational KPIs.
synthesis.contribution: Provides a structured framework for what to log in LLM apps, how to build privacy-safe telemetry, and which operational KPIs to track across interaction, execution, performance, and safety layers to support fault detection, cost management, reliability, and enterprise implementation.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as central evidence for the operational governance strand on observability, logging, telemetry, auditability, privacy-safe monitoring, and KPI-based oversight of LLM applications in regulated or enterprise contexts; pair with empirical implementation studies because this source appears conceptual in the material provided.

evidence.claim: Article focuses specifically on LLM applications and enterprise conversational use cases.
evidence.excerpt: Large Language Model (LLM) applications increasingly form an integral part of enterprise software architecture, enabling conversational interfaces, intelligent assistant applications, and autonomous decision-support systems.

evidence.claim: Traditional observability is insufficient for governance and semantic monitoring of LLMs.
evidence.excerpt: The traditional approach to observability, relying on logs, metrics, and traces, is found to be inadequate to measure semantic correctness, behavioral consistency, and governance risks associated with LLM applications.

evidence.claim: Study proposes a conceptual observability framework from three viewpoints.
evidence.excerpt: This study explores the concept of observability in large language model (LLM) applications from three different viewpoints: auditable data selection, privacy-preserving telemetry construction, and meaningful operational key performance indicator (KPI) definition.

evidence.claim: Framework is model-agnostic and organized into four layers.
evidence.excerpt: the study proposes a conceptual framework for model-agnostic observability in LLMs that covers the interaction layer, execution layer, performance layer, and safety layer.
the study focuses on the application of privacy by design, including metadata-centric logging, selective redaction, and controlled access to telemetry data.

evidence.claim: Operational KPIs include reliability, efficiency, output quality, and safety compliance.
evidence.excerpt: this paper introduces a well- defined set of operational key performance indicators (KPIs) specific to large language model (LLM) applications, including reliability, performance efficiency, measures of output quality, and safety compliance.

evidence.claim: Keywords explicitly tie the work to AI system governance.
evidence.excerpt: KEYWORDS Large Language Models (LLMs), Observability, Privacy-Safe Telemetry, Operational Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), AI System Governance

evidence.claim: LLM apps may handle regulated or sensitive content, raising governance concerns.
evidence.excerpt: Large Language Model (LLM) applications often need to manage user data, confidential information, and regulated content. This raises significant concerns

evidence.claim: Research type is framework-oriented rather than empirical in the provided text.
evidence.excerpt: Following the best practices of software observability and MLOps, the study proposes a conceptual framework for model-agnostic observability in LLMs
